title: Army Weekly Briefing
description: Army leadership, force design, modernization, contracts and the signal and network enterprise.
readFirst: Covers Nov. 9–16. New: Stars and Stripes reported Nov. 13 that soldiers at Grafenwoehr tested containerized drones and unmanned ground vehicles, including a swarm of 18 drones, and Army.mil reported Nov. 12 that PADDS users have moved onto the Army Contract Writing System. An EIN Presswire copy of a 25th Infantry Division release described a Nov. 13 HIMARS live fire at Kwajalein, but the original DVIDS or Army.mil article was not opened, so it was not added. No new NETCOM release and no new Army enterprise agreement were found in Army CIO reporting, ESI, Federal News Network, Breaking Defense, DefenseScoop, Nextgov, GovConWire, or vendor newsrooms. No confirmation that Brig. Gen. Sutten assumed command of CECOM on Nov. 16 was found; the Oct. 28 town hall note aged out. The Week Ahead subsection is empty.

items.headline: CNBC: British police arrest a U.S. Army soldier on suspicion of spying for Russia
items.summary: CNBC reported Nov. 11 that London's Metropolitan Police said a 41-year-old U.S. Army soldier was arrested near Gloucester, England, on Tuesday on suspicion of spying for Russia, and that he is being held under the U.K. National Security Act. CNBC said a senior NATO official confirmed the soldier was assigned to the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps in Gloucestershire, and that police worked with U.S. military authorities and the FBI. FBI Director Kash Patel said the allegations were of the utmost concern, and Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, said the alleged conduct is a reminder that insider threats are real. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that Moscow had absolutely nothing to do with the case.

items.headline: Grafenwoehr test fires containerized drone swarms and robotic Javelin launchers
items.summary: Stars and Stripes reported Nov. 13 that soldiers at Grafenwoehr Training Area on Thursday attacked targets with weapons stored in shipping containers, drones, and unmanned vehicles. The demonstration began with an unmanned ground vehicle carrying two Javelin launchers, and another unmanned ground vehicle then fired a swarm of 18 drones from a pre-positioned container. Col. Michael Weisman, a senior spokesman for the Army in Europe, said in a statement Friday that the systems are part of the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative. Alex Tomosieski of the Combat Capabilities Development Command said the Army wants to store drones and unmanned ground vehicles in containers under a program called the Remote Rapid Response Contingency Team.

items.headline: Army Materiel Command says small attack drones will be replaced, not stockpiled
items.summary: Breaking Defense reported Nov. 12 that Jon Strzelec, Army Materiel Command's advanced manufacturing lead for small drones, said the Army told his team that small drones will not be stored on shelves and that the service will manufacture to deliver, not to stock. He said a countermeasure can appear within 72 hours in Ukraine, and that building a new drone is cheaper than pulling a circuit card, flashing software, and returning the aircraft to service. He said the Army was receiving 10,000 of the first 30,000 small drones from Drone Dominance Gauntlet 1, and that those aircraft go to units for training and are not sustained after they break. He said Group 2 drones, which he described as 21 to 55 pounds and used for reconnaissance or delivery, are more likely to be kept in service because the mission and the cost are different.

items.headline: Breaking Defense: launched effects are with 11 of 12 divisions, mostly from Griffon
items.summary: Breaking Defense reported Nov. 9 that the Army has fielded launched effects to 11 of its 12 headquarters divisions and to each multi-domain task force. Lt. Col. Hunter Gray, product manager for launched effects, told reporters Thursday that the fielding follows Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's 2025 Drone Dominance memo, which directed those systems to every headquarters division and multi-domain task force by the end of 2026, and that the 12th division is due to start receiving them next month. Gray said Griffon Aerospace can provide hundreds of systems a month and that the majority of what has been delivered is long-range capability from Griffon, including its Outlaw drone. He said payloads include intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, electronic warfare, and kinetic effects, and he did not disclose which divisions have the systems.

items.headline: Army moves PADDS users onto the Army Contract Writing System
items.summary: Army.mil reported Nov. 12, datelined Fort Belvoir, that the Army retired the Standard Procurement System earlier in fiscal 2026 and migrated users and contract actions from the Procurement Automated Data and Document System to the Army Contract Writing System. During the fiscal year-end surge the system migrated over 20,000 contract files in 90 days and trained over 1,100 users in the fourth quarter, and as of Oct. 1 more than 9,600 contracting professionals worldwide had access. Doug Haskin, project manager at Capability Program Executive Enterprise Software and Services, said the platform lets the Army respond more rapidly to emerging requirements. Lt. Col. Camille Morgan, product manager for the system, said migrating thousands of legacy files protected warfighter procurement needs while building an audit-ready enterprise, and final PADDS decommissioning continues through late 2026.

items.headline: Safe Pro says the Army awarded $2.5 million to put threat detection on Ghost-X
items.summary: Safe Pro Group said Nov. 10 that the U.S. Army awarded it a $2.5 million prime contract under a Commercial Solutions Opening for Ground Threat Detection through Aerial Reconnaissance, and that the work is the company's first prime contract. Safe Pro said the contract puts its Ground Truth Air software on Anduril's Ghost-X drone to identify and geolocate more than 150 types of explosive threats, including landmines, anti-personnel mines, cluster munitions, and ambush first-person-view drones, and to stream that data into ATAK and Anduril's Lattice. The company said the Army selected Ghost-X for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance under the Medium Range Reconnaissance program. Daniel Leighton, Anduril's general manager of tactical effects, said the addition is meant to support tank survivability and reconnaissance. The release does not name a period of performance or the units that will use the software.

items.headline: Army.mil: JIATF-401 awards DroneSec a contract for unmanned-systems threat intelligence
items.summary: Army.mil reported Nov. 10 that the Department of War, through Joint Interagency Task Force 401, awarded a contract to DroneSec for intelligence products and threat analysis on adversary unmanned systems. The article says the work covers emerging technologies, procurement networks, and the tactics used to develop and employ weaponized drones, and that the task force will use DroneSec's open-source intelligence to inform capability development and counter-drone planning. Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, director of JIATF-401, said understanding how unmanned systems are developed is required to keep an advantage. The release does not state a dollar value.

items.headline: 25th Infantry Division says it is pushing next-gen command-and-control compute to company level
items.summary: The Department of War reported Nov. 12 that the 25th Infantry Division and partners are in Joint Pacific Multinational Readiness Center Rotation 27-01 in Hawaii, after the 11th Airborne Division flew 300 paratroopers 3,000 miles from Alaska. Maj. Gen. Jeff VanAntwerp, the division commander, said the 25th is one of two next-generation command-and-control-enabled divisions and that its cloud-based architecture pushes a good amount of compute from brigades down to the company level. He said the division is adding a secure network on top of mesh radios and commercially available devices so dispersed units have more computing power and tools for commanders. In the Lightning Surge 6 exercise, soldiers are limiting electronic transmissions at night and testing whether they can stay connected on tactical mesh radios and secure, unclassified data layers ahead of a long-range maritime air assault.

items.headline: Breaking Defense: a CNAS fellow says NGC2 has to connect nodes thousands of miles apart
items.summary: Breaking Defense reported Nov. 11 an interview with Josh Wallin, a defense program fellow at the Center for a New American Security, on the Army's Next Generation Command and Control effort. Wallin said an Indo-Pacific fight raises the problem of connecting systems that may be thousands of miles apart, and that bandwidth is strained by the volume of transmissions needed to keep distributed forces synchronized. He said NGC2 is trying to separate data links and radios from compute and from the data layer, so a jammed satellite terminal could be swapped without rebuilding the software above it. He also said the Army wants data that used to sit in separate air-defense, logistics, and fires systems to be usable across functions, with artificial intelligence used to automate parts of analysis that are still manual.
